title: Russell Brand was a 'sexual predator', prosecution alleges as rape trial begins
content: Russell Brand was described as "ruthless" and a "sexual predator" by the prosecution at the start of his trial for rape and sexual assault on Wednesday. The 51-year-old actor and comedian faces three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges. Riel Karmy-Jones KC, for the prosecution, told Southwark Crown Court in London the women "did not know each other", "have never met each other" and "came forward independently of each other". The barrister said: "The circumstances of the offending were as wide and as varied as the defendant's career." She said that "regardless of who the women were and what they said or did, Brand was not deterred". "His desire, strong desire, for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious," she told the court. The prosecutor told jurors that Brand would be "nice when he wanted to be, funny - undoubtedly - charming, likeable even, when he wanted something in return". But she said he would also be "demanding, entitled, a flirt with a huge sexual appetite - childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met". The prosecutor said Brand would "appear indifferent, normal and untroubled by what had just occurred" after the encounters. She added that "sometimes he would leave promptly after the incident, sometimes making an excuse to get away, or sometimes simply continuing as though nothing wrong had happened". On Wednesday, the jury heard details of the alleged offences. The first complainant says she met Brand before he was famous in 1999, the jury was told. She had attended the Labour Party conference and went to a fringe event where she spoke to Brand. He later allegedly raped her. The prosecution said when Brand was questioned by police about this allegation of rape, "he said if it happened, he didn't remember the incident". He added that he did not remember the first complainant's name and that he "had never engaged in non-consensual activity". The second complainant worked for MTV at the time when she says Brand indecently assaulted her. She said Brand asked her where the toilets were and the woman offered to show him. When they reached the toilets, prosecutors say, Brand asked the woman to "come in" before grabbing her forearm. She resisted by struggling and pulling back. He had what she described as a desperate, wild-eyed look on his face, as he said: "Please please come in – oh go on." The third complainant says Brand orally raped her in a toilet after meeting her at a party in 2004. Within a minute of meeting, in the middle of a conversation, he lurched forward and grabbed her breasts and squeezed them with both hands, the jury was told. The prosecution said the woman remembered he had a "big, weird grin" on his face as he did so, then grabbed her arm and pulled her towards the toilets. The same woman said that as they were driving to another venue, Brand exposed himself, the court heard. "He said, 'Come on, come on, suck it' – to which she just said, 'No no'," the prosecution added. "He simply laughed but appeared to accept her refusal." The fourth complainant says Brand pushed her up against a wall at Capital Radio in 2004 or 2005 and kissed her "sloppily and aggressively", and "grabbed her body, at her breasts, sides and buttocks, aggressively". She was able to push him away and he "just sniggered, like it was a joke", the prosecutor said. The jury then heard how the fifth complainant says she met Brand when he was performing at the Hammersmith Apollo in London in 2009. The prosecution said their encounter began with consensual activity, but that he raped her anally on a later occasion. The jury heard how the woman "spent months and years blaming herself", becoming anxious and unwell. They were told Brand texted the woman after seeing her at an event the following summer, saying: "I wanna push you further." She is said to have replied: "I think you pushed me far enough – you treated me like an animal." He allegedly replied: "I'm sorry." The sixth complainant - who has accused Brand of sexual assault - says he demanded a massage when she was on a work assignment in 2009. He "fell to his knees and placed his head directly into her groin area", the prosecution said. After the accounts of the final two women were heard, the prosecutor said Brand told police in 2023 "he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity, and that any accounts had been reinvented or imagined after a defamatory documentary and subsequent press reporting". The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks. Brand was accompanied by his wife Laura to the court on Wednesday. He rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music. He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States. The TV presenter says she suffered memory loss following her operation to remove a benign tumour. Davis was found guilty last month over his role in the late rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in 1996. title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
content: A Ukrainian man has gone on trial in Hamburg accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany, four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history. Prosecutors say Serhii Kuznetsov played a leading role in a team of saboteurs that destroyed the pipelines, accusing him of a war crime. His defence has called for the case to be dismissed. The case is highly sensitive in Germany, one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place. Extradited to Germany last year, Kuznetsov denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia. Kuznetsov became the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts on Wednesday morning, and a packed public gallery looked on as he entered the courtroom, appearing relaxed. He even smiled at times, including during initial exchanges where he spoke to confirm personal details such as his name and place of birth. He had previously only been identified by German prosecutors as Serhii K and pictured with his face blurred, before the court lifted an anonymity order on Wednesday. Kuznetsov, 50, wore a pair of headphones and appeared to listen intently to a translation of proceedings in Ukrainian, as the prosecution read out the charges against him of ordering divers and an explosive expert to attack civilian infrastructure. The defence outlined their case, telling the court that only circumstantial evidence had emerged in the four years since the Nord Stream blasts. "[Prosecutors] made a thorough investigation of four years," Italian defence lawyer Nicola Canestrini told the BBC outside the courtroom. "They did not find one single witness, they did not find no forensics, no DNA, no fingerprints - nothing!" Canestrini and his colleagues argued that as a soldier the defendant was bound to secrecy, and therefore he could not have a fair trial as he was unable to defend himself. "Let's say he has an alibi, he was on another secret operation, how can you prove that if he's [not able] to tell us as defence attorneys where he was and which witnesses we could summon?" Prosecutors argue the case falls under Germany's code of crimes against international law as a war crime, as an "attack by military means against civilian objects". The defence told the court his extradition to Germany was flawed as no mention had been made at the time of the war crime allegation. In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame. Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts. As investigators from Sweden, Denmark and Germany tried to find out who carried out the attack, Russia's Vladimir Putin accused the US and its UK allies, blaming "the Anglo-Saxons" - which they denied. Eventually, after Denmark and Sweden shut down their inquiries, German prosecutors focused on a group of deep-sea divers who had rented a yacht called the Andromeda in the northern German port of Rostock. They said later that "traces of subsea explosives were found in the samples taken from the boat". Despite the strain on relations with Kyiv, German prosecutors pressed ahead with the case, and in January 2025 the German federal court of justice ruled that it fell within German territorial jurisdiction and prosecutors had a responsibility to act as it involved "undermining [Germany's] internal security". Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has always maintained that Ukraine had "nothing to do with [the Nord Stream blasts]", although in their indictment German prosecutors allege the saboteurs conceived the plot "acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies". The case has highlighted differences of opinion on the trial in Kyiv and Berlin. Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee in the Ukrainian parliament, points out that the blasts took place during a time of war with Russia and "Nord Stream 2 was nothing but a tool used by Russia in order to get prepared for the war". He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions." However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case. "They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained. In August 2025, Kuznetsov was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany. After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, when his surname emerged in court documents, Kuznetsov was transferred to Germany late last year. German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army , and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert. While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court. In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just". Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage. Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial. Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us". title: Hidden video recording device found in cabin of Australian navy ship
content: A hidden video recording device has been found in an Australian navy ship's cabin, the Australian Defence Force (ADF) has confirmed. The device was located on Sunday in the cabin of Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin in Cairns, Queensland. The confirmation came after independent Australian senator Jacqui Lambie, a former veteran and defence advocate, told parliament she was contacted by personnel with allegations that "concealed cameras have recently been found in the female sailors' showers facilities". Australia's defence department has not said whether the device was found in a female-only space and said the incident was referred to the Joint Military Police United. Lambie told the Australian Senate on Wednesday: "I was also told this had occurred recently and prevented the vessel from sailing while investigations were ongoing. Even more disturbing are claims that footage from these cameras may have been uploaded online before the cameras were discovered. "How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask navy." Later on Wednesday, the defence department confirmed it became aware of a video recording device being found in a HMAS Leeuwin cabin but did not give specific details on where it was discovered. "Defence takes this incident extremely seriously and does not tolerate unacceptable behaviour in any form," the department said in its statement. "The ship remained alongside to enable the investigation and ensure immediate support was provided to members of the ship's crew. The welfare of individuals remains Defence's priority, and support is ongoing. "As the matter is currently under investigation and to protect the privacy of the affected individuals, Defence is unable to provide further comment at this time." title: India's 'cockroach' leaders jailed after holding protest
content: Two top leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) have been sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka appeared before a magistrate on Wednesday after being detained at Jantar Mantar, a longstanding venue for demonstrations that police recently removed from the city's list of authorised protest sites. The two were among a group who climbed a locked gate and crossed barricades to enter the site on Tuesday. The GenZ-led movement has been protesting for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud - charges the poll panel denies. Police accused Das, Ranka and their fellow activist Ajinkya Shinde of trespassing, breaching a peace bond, violating prohibitory orders and obstructing public officials - charges they deny. Delhi's Special Executive Magistrate Court remanded Das and Ranka to five days in judicial custody, while Shinde was released on a personal bond. The two leaders can seek bail from a higher court. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who has been holding separate protests against the Election Commission, condemned the arrests, describing them as "an act of cowardice", and expressed support for peaceful demonstrations at Jantar Mantar. "Students. Youth. Journalists. The [opposition's] INDIA bloc. Different banners, one cause. All protests are one: citizens demanding their constitutional rights," he wrote on X. Other leaders of the opposition, like former chief ministers of West Bengal and Delhi- Mamata Banerjee and Arvind Kejriwal respectively - also took to X to extend support to CJP and condemn the arrest of its leaders. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who was travelling to Delhi after the arrests, accused the government of cracking down on dissent and challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to "declare the Emergency officially", according to news agency PTI. His comments drew parallels with India's 1970s Emergency, a period when civil liberties were curtailed under then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. The CJP, which is a pressure group and not an official political party, has been demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing. Wednesday's actions follow a weekend of protests during which Das, Ranka, Shinde, and Dipke were taken into preventive custody ahead of planned demonstrations at Jantar Mantar. They were later released by a magistrate. Police imposed extensive security restrictions across Delhi, closing several metro stations and deploying thousands of police and paramilitary personnel to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site. Thousands of people, including journalists, were detained and later released, while videos showed police forcibly dragging some protesters into buses. Following the weekend protests, Delhi police removed Jantar Mantar from its list of authorised protest sites, instead designating three other venues - Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground. The CJP criticised the decision, saying it would make demonstrations less visible and harder for protesters to make their voices heard. On Tuesday, the activists returned to Jantar Mantar despite the restrictions. Videos shared by Dipke and other CJP leaders showed Das and Ranka climbing over police barricades, carrying Indian flags and chanting slogans. "You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X. Ratna Singh, head of the CJP's legal team, alleged that the activists were denied access to lawyers for several hours before being taken to Parliament Street Police Station in a private vehicle at about 03:00 local time (21:30 GMT on Tuesday). She also rejected a police allegation that CJP leaders had called on others to join the protest at Jantar Mantar. "Absolutely false! No public call was ever made," she wrote on X. The CJP emerged from student-led demonstrations earlier this year over alleged exam irregularities and demands for education reforms. Weeks of protests led by the movement culminated in the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The group began as an online satire movement after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches during a court hearing in May. He later said his remarks had been misinterpreted, but the comments had already become a rallying cry for young people demanding change. Following the summer protests, the CJP developed into a wider pressure group, tapping into discontent over unemployment, examinations and government accountability. The CJP launched its latest nationwide protests in Mumbai on 2 October, following an Indian Express report alleging that Chief Election Commissioner Kumar had ignored objections from his two fellow commissioners over changes to voter registration. The newspaper reported that commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised concerns at least 14 times over 10 months about decisions taken without their knowledge, including changes affecting voter databases and electoral rolls. The Election Commission has denied the allegations, saying its decisions were unanimous. The controversy has intensified scrutiny of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, a voter verification exercise that opposition parties allege has benefited Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission and the government denies this. Although the CJP and opposition parties have not held joint protests, their demonstrations have coincided in recent days. Gandhi is among politicians, lawyers and journalists detained during protests across several cities. title: Australia's first-ever Michelin stars go to 11 restaurants in one state
content: Australia has been awarded its first Michelin stars, with 11 restaurants in the state of South Australia receiving the distinction. Magill Estate Restaurant in Adelaide was the only venue to receive two stars, while 10 others were awarded one star each. South Australia's government paid for incognito inspectors to visit the state, according to national broadcaster ABC, which is why no spots have been recognised in other parts of the country. The announcement comes more than a century after the Michelin Guide was first published in France and following years of unsuccessful attempts to bring it to Australia. Michelin has approached the national tourism board several times about bringing the guide to the country with no success. South Australia decided to go it alone and pursued its own deal. The state government has not disclosed how much it paid, but Tourism Minister Emily Bourke defended the investment in an interview with ABC News. "It is enabling us to create a tourism destination and put us on the world map," she said. The move follows Michelin's expansion into New Zealand, which became the first destination in Oceania to feature in the guide in July, agreeing to pay NZ$6.3m (£2.7m; $3.5m) over three years for its inclusion. Created by brothers André and Édouard Michelin in 1900, the guide was originally designed to encourage motorists to travel - ultimately boosting their core business of selling tyres. It offered drivers maps and recommendations for places to eat and stay, before evolving into one of the best-known names in restaurant recognition. Michelin stars were introduced in 1926 and have since become a major distinction for chefs and restaurants around the world. One star recognises high-quality cooking, two stars indicate excellent cooking worth a detour, while three stars are reserved for exceptional cuisine worth a special journey. Among the one-star recipients is Arkhé in Norwood, which specialises in open-fire cooking, while Aptos in Adelaide serves a tasting menu focused on native Australian ingredients. Here is the full list: Two Michelin stars One Michelin star The wider guide includes more than 70 other South Australian restaurants, with some recognised through the Bib Gourmand category, which highlights restaurants offering good food at more moderate prices. title: Saudi Arabia overturns death sentence for man over Facebook comment, Sri Lanka says
content: Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court has set aside the death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan migrant worker over a comment he made on Facebook, Colombo's Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra said. Anojan Sivarasa, 27, was sentenced to death in September after a Saudi appellate court convicted him of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over his comment. The case sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka , spurring diplomatic efforts to seek clemency. Saudi Arabia's top court set aside the sentence on Wednesday, Hemachandra said in a post on Facebook, where he thanked the authorities and legal teams of both nations for their efforts. In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online. During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Sivarasa to respond in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad. Although Sivarasa promptly deleted the comment and posted an apology video, a screenshot of it was brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July. It is not clear if there will be further legal proceedings or whether Sivarasa will remain in detention, and for how long. He was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of three million Saudi riyals ($0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court. Faizer Mustafa, a Sri Lankan lawmaker who is involved in legal negotiations with Saudi Arabia regarding Sivarasa's case, confirmed to BBC Sinhala that Saudi Arabia had overturned the death sentence, adding that they are reviewing the Supreme Court's latest ruling. Sivarasa's family had earlier said they have had no direct contact with him since 28 September. International rights groups had also joined calls for Saudi to spare his life. "Saudi authorities should end their use of abusive laws to hand out extraordinary sentences for speech-related offenses, especially against migrant workers who are already in a vulnerable position with limited protections," Joey Shea, senior Saudi Arabia researcher at Human Rights Watch, said on Tuesday. The Saudi energy ministry says the Houthi attack caused a "limited fire" at Aramco's headquarters complex in Dhahran. title: 'Multiple searches' after four arson attack murders
content: Searches have been carried out at a number of premises in Waterford after four members of the same family were killed in an arson attack in the city. Kim English, Philip English and two of their children - nine-year-old Jayden and 12-year-old Callum - died after their home in Birch Avenue was set on fire on Tuesday. Gardaí (Irish police) have described the investigation into their murders as "intense in nature and very active". They said "multiple searches" were conducted on Tuesday evening and a number of vehicles and electronic devices have been seized for technical examination. Six members of the English family were sleeping when their home was attacked in the early hours of Tuesday. It is believed that an incendiary device, likely a petrol bomb, set the house on fire. Two children were severely injured in the blaze and were taken to a Dublin hospital where they both remain in a critical condition. Members of the local community have been supporting their relatives and some have been sharing poignant memories of those who did not survive the fire. For the past five years, Callum played football for Johnville FC, a schoolboy and junior football club in Waterford. His coach Alex O'Sullivan told BBC News NI that he was a "fantastic player" and a "lovely kid" both on and off the pitch. "Great sense of humour... always happy. Helpful to his teammates and coaches. There was never any cheek coming from Callum. "You'd often see him on the street and he'd be waving, 'Hello coach', and you'd get a little chat out of him, and he always had a great smile on his face." O'Sullivan said he first met Callum when he was playing under-11s football. "Callum was always there. Same with matches, he loved coming to the matches." O'Sullivan said he also got to know the boy's parents Phillip and Kim, from dropping Callum off to training and supporting him when he was playing. "They were always there to show up." Jayden was born with a heart condition and travelled to appointments in Dublin by BUMBLEance, a children's ambulance service. Waterford based paramedic Áine Phelan worked with the service and had travelled with Jayden to his appointments, Irish broadcaster RTÉ has reported. She told the broadcaster it was an "absolute privilege" to accompany Jayden and she was trying to comprehend what has happened. Phelan added that her thoughts are with the family in the "sad, sad days ahead". Amanda Powney was friends with Kim and Phillip, and her son got the school bus with Jayden. Powney said she looked after the children so she has "known them since they were tiny tots". She described Jayden as a happy boy adding that he was "full of his fun", adding that it the situation is "very sad". Gabija Gataveckaite, Dublin correspondent, BBC News NI, in Waterford The community in Waterford city is in shock following the fatal fire which claimed four lives. Butler's Community Centre is operating a drop-in service for any members of the community who may need support or help to process the grief. Normally, the community centre is a location for sporting, cultural and family events. But on Tuesday it has been turned into a service to support the grieving community. Supports on offer include the Health Service Executive (HSE) and charities Bernardos and Jigsaw as well as the local council. The centre is just a stone's throw from Birchwood, the estate where the family lived. Neighbours brought flowers to the house and passed them onto gardaí who are still preserving the scene. They were visibly emotional and shaken as they gathered in small groups around the estate. James English, who was 12-year-old Callum's godfather said the family is "not too good". "We have a loss of a family now, wiped out. Please whoever done it, own up," he told reporters. There are many gardai and investigating officers at the estate as the murder investigation continues. O'Sullivan said the community and club were "devastated". "There has been a dark cloud over St John's Park. "Usually there's always people with a smile on their face around St John's Park. Everyone is sad today." In a statement on social media, Johnville FC said all its members were "absolutely heartbroken" "It is incredibly difficult to comprehend that a family we knew so well has been taken from us in such tragic circumstances." The Catholic Diocese of Waterford and Lismore has confirmed that a vigil will be held at Sacred Heart Church on Wednesday evening. In a post on social media, the diocese said the vigil will provide an opportunity for people to "come together in prayer for those who have lost their lives, their grieving families and loved ones, and all those affected by this terrible tragedy". Gardaí launched an investigation into the four killings on Tuesday, describing it as a "multiple murder and arson attack". Irish broadcaster RTÉ is reporting that detectives believe the attack is linked to organised crime and drugs-related intimidation. It said the searches carried out in the city on Tuesday night included raids on properties of two significant criminal figures in the city. No arrests have been made as yet. On Wednesday, Ch Supt Anthony Pettit said: "There are people in the community who know the person or persons who carried out this arson attack in which four people have been murdered." He appealed for them to contact the investigation team, which is based at Waterford Garda Station. On Tuesday morning, firefighters, ambulance staff and gardaí all responded to the emergency at the family home in the Birchwood housing estate, about 3km (1.8 miles) outside Waterford city centre. Waterford Fire Service said it was alerted to the fire at 05:13 local time and its crews arrived to a well-developed fire at a two-storey house. It said a number of casualties were removed from the house before the blaze was extinguished and the scene was handed over to gardaí. On Tuesday afternoon, Ch Supt Pettit said officers believe the house "was attacked by a person or persons unknown and that the fire was started deliberately". He appealed to anyone who was in the vicinity of the Birchwood housing estate between 04.30 and 05.30 local time on Tuesday morning to contact gardaí. It comes amidst an an ongoing pay dispute between public sector workers and the Irish government. Ten people died in the blast at a petrol station in Creeslough, County Donegal, on 7 October 2022. Gary Anderson had been serving life in prison for the murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry in 2018. He is charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017. Ireland Fashion Week is under way with more than 80 designers showcasing their work. title: Pakistan has locked down Imran Khan's stronghold - but it could backfire
content: Schools closed. The internet partially shut. Roads blocked by shipping containers. And the army arriving in town. Imran Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, is under a state of emergency, his party's provincial government suspended. It's another dramatic escalation in the standoff between the former prime minister's supporters and Pakistan's state - and one that some fear could lead to more instability, not less. According to the federal government this step, allowed by the constitution, was needed to provide protection for the province's population from the threat of terror. "The PTI KPK government was hand in glove with the terrorists," Attah Tarrar, federal information minister, told journalists on Sunday. He did not elaborate or provide evidence, but promised to do so soon. Two days later there had still been no update from him - but schools had reopened in Peshawar and most parts of the province, and internet services had been restored. While police would not confirm any detentions, there is clearly a crackdown under way to prevent protests. Most PTI leaders in the province have gone into hiding. On Tuesday dozens of PTI supporters took to the streets in Bara, Khyber district, hometown of provincial Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. There were reports of tear gas shelling in the area. To many observers, the timing of Sunday's announcement of emergency rule is not coincidental. For the last week, thousands of Imran Khan's supporters have marched through Khyber Pakhtunkhwa , where the PTI have been in power for 13 years, demanding Khan's release. "The charitable response would be to say that it sounded disingenuous," says Farzana Sheikh, associate fellow at Chatham House. "I do not see the link with terrorism," says Arifa Noor, journalist and commentator. "I'm not even sure if it was the long march itself [that led to this]. Perhaps it was the last straw or perhaps it's just a case of saying, we don't want to deal with the government being in the hands of an opposition party." The protests were led by Chief Minister Afridi, whose whereabouts are still a mystery. His party says he has been arrested; the government says that he is in protective custody. Before the march had begun, there had been a crackdown. Three of Khan's sisters were arrested in September , accused among other things of mobilising supporters, and have been detained ever since. Khan has barely been seen by his family or lawyers in the last year; two of his sisters saw him in August, one in prison, another as he was checked over at a hospital visit after concerns were raised by the Supreme Court about his health, before he was returned behind bars again where he has been held for more than three years. The PTI leader, who is widely believed to have lost power because of a rift with Pakistan's powerful military, has been imprisoned since August 2023. He is convicted in several corruption cases which he says are politically motivated. With the party already weakened, why this reaction from the authorities? "The PTI rank and file has been becoming increasingly restless in recent months amid growing concerns about Imran Khan's health," says Michael Kugelman, senior South Asia fellow at the Atlantic Council. "There is a sense that perhaps now is the time to send a very strong message to the party and make it more difficult for them to be able to put pressure on the government." The government has previously argued that Khan was going against jail rules by using his meetings to discuss politics. Tarar has said of the state of emergency: "There was no political agenda. They could have gone on with their march," and pointed to the talks the two sides had in the run-up to the decision as an indicator that they did try discussion. But others see this as just another attempt to restrict Khan and his party. "The government has less and less space for disagreements or dissent and they do not want to negotiate their way out of any kind of conflict," Noor says. Zahid Hussain, Islamabad-based author and defence analyst, is clear about who is behind the decision. "The balance of power is completely shifted to the military establishment," he says. Sheikh thinks that Pakistan's military is feeling confident because it believes it has a good relationship with the White House, its international credentials burnished by their role in the US-Iran peace talks. "The mode is very much, this is the moment, let's seize it," she says. "There is a sense that, we have all the cards in our hands. We can ride this out internationally." But Pakistan has plenty to contend with. Militancy is rising. The country was ranked number one in the Global Terrorism Index 2026 as the country which had been affected most. The country is at loggerheads with two neighbours; it has repeatedly hit Afghanistan with air strikes accusing the Afghan Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, a claim it denies. It would take little to reignite its long-running simmering conflict with India. Meanwhile, it has promised to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against attacks as the conflict against the Houthis has become increasingly dangerous. Short of solving one problem, some have warned this state of emergency could lead to more challenges. It risks increasing political instability, with Islamabad taking responsibility for a province without a buffer - the provincial government - they can blame. "I would argue that this could actually backfire," Kugelman says. "You're playing with fire because if this move ends up adding to the anger and the discontent among so many there, then you have a very big problem on your hands." "It is reckless, given the challenges, multiple challenges the country is facing," Hussain says. He fears that more of these powers could be used across Pakistan. Attempts to combat militancy with more active army operations could come with its own perils too, Sheikh argues. "If they're going to launch these operations, they're going to have to be prepared to accept casualties of members of the armed forces," she says. If those are significant, it could lead to questions inside the military institution, she adds. Pakistan, with its history of military coups, has examples in its past where removing elected governments, whether provincial or national, can turn sour. "It's not that senior people in the PML-N [the party in federal government] don't realise that some of these things can come back and haunt them in the future," Noor says. "Similarly I think to some extent the PTI realises that they will not be able to hold a protest and get Imran Khan out. I think that's the most unfortunate part of this mess that we're in, that we are going into it with our eyes wide open. "Everybody realises that this is a train crash but somehow you can't stop it." Thousands have taken to the streets after talks between authorities and Khan's party ended in deadlock. Aleema Khanum is accused of mobilising her brother’s supporters ahead of country-wide protests. The former skippers say it is "basic decency" for Pakistan to comply with a court-ordered medical assessment. It comes as the court had earlier this week ordered that he had to be taken for a hospital examination. Imran Khan has been imprisoned since 2023 on corruption charges which he says were politically motivated. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children'
content: In China's cities, despite the huge crowds, or maybe because of them, residents can feel very isolated. Now, a new industry being dubbed the "loneliness economy" has emerged, with people hiring themselves out as companions to help the elderly. The BBC's China correspondent Stephen McDonell visits a company that does just that, to see how their business works. Read more about the paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely. Reports say a gas leak at a fried chicken shop may be behind the blast, which killed two and injured 26. With Super Tuesday underway in the US, the BBC asks China's elite who they want to win this year's election. At least nine people were injured in the incident, which Chinese state media said involved over 100 cars. A trained economist, Li was once tipped to be the country's future leader. The highest level of storm alert is in effect in Hong Kong, with people being warned to stay indoors. China police issue warnings after a child is seen playing hide and seek on the side of a apartment building. Giant panda at Wolong Shenshuping, China, looks very relaxed whilst they have the hiccups Video from China’s Sichuan province shows the animal looking relaxed, but unimpressed. The rescue was shown on Chinese state TV as devastating floods hit Hebei province. Parts of China have been hit by an onslaught of extreme weather, causing widespread flooding. This video has been removed for rights reasons. The blast was caused by a leaking liquefied petroleum gas tank, state media reports. Harrowing video shows people trying to escape a fire in Beijing that killed 29 people. On land, by sea and in the air - pictures released by China's state broadcaster show military drills around Taiwan. The BBC's Celia Hatton breaks down Xi Jinping's caffeine habits, and why they might be a subtle power play. As China deals with a new Covid wave, Ros Atkins looks at why it’s hard to assess its scale. Jimmy and Tommy Lindesay are covering the equivalent of a marathon every day for six months. People in Beijing see a cautious return to life after China lifts its most severe Covid restrictions. There were widespread protests after 10 people died in a tower block fire in the city of Urumqi. title: Pictured: Winning entries for Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026
content: An emotional scene of an elephant carrying a deceased calf has earned Italian photographer Federico Veronesi the title of Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026. While tracking elephants in Namibia's Huab River Valley, Veronesi spotted an unusual trail of drag marks across the sand of a dry riverbed. Following the tracks, he came across a female elephant carrying a dead calf, its leg wedged between her tusk and trunk. Initially, Veronesi assumed the elephant was the calf's mother. But after sharing his photographs with an elephant research project working in the area, he learned that this wasn't certain. Researchers recognised the elephant as a female who had lost a calf several years earlier and said she had previously picked up dead calves belonging to other females. For Veronesi, the encounter was deeply significant. "Of all the 20 years I've done photographing animals, this is the most heart-wrecking and fascinating and dramatic," he said, describing it as "revealing of the depth and complexity of the emotions, the feelings of the animals." He hopes the image will encourage people to look beyond animals' physical appearance and recognise them as individuals with their own relationships, memories and emotions. "It's a small window that opens just a crack into the complexity of their world," he said. The competition's annual exhibition opens at the Natural History Museum on Friday 16 October 2026. Keep scrolling to see more award-winning images. Category : Young Grand Title and 11 to 14 Years Photographer : Oscar Whitfield, Zimbabwe/UK Location : Zambezi National Park, Zimbabwe Only by lying in the dust and capturing the beetle at eye level could Whitfield show how much strength its task required. While on a family game drive in Zimbabwe, near his home in Victoria Falls, he spotted the dung beetle struggling to push a ball of dung uphill through the sand, with a trail of flies following closely behind. After experimenting with different angles and compositions, he captured a moment that reveals the extraordinary effort involved in this seemingly simple task. "I hope that when people look at the photograph, they can see too, and maybe appreciate how much can be happening in a small moment in the natural world," says Whitfield. Category : 10 Years and Under Photographer : Amelie Davis, UK Location : Surrey, England You do not need a camera or a plane ticket to take an award-winning photo. Davis captured this shot in the garden using her dad's smartphone. The image freezes in time a single wingbeat from a common carder bumblebee as it prepares to land on a flower. Category : Animals in their Environment Photographer : James Lewin, UK Location : Chyulu Hills National Park, Kenya Lewin captured this dreamy, black-and-white photo of a young bull elephant spraying zebras at a waterhole. He softened the usually harsh light by using a camera converted to infrared. Category : Animal Portraits Photographer : Aaron Sanders, UK Location : Porthkerris Beach, Cornwall Common octopuses are usually found in the warmer Mediterranean Sea. But with global warming pushing up springtime sea temperatures, sightings across south-west England have massively increased. Sanders described the moment he spotted a single eye peeking from behind the kelp: "We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity." Category : Birds Photographer : Isak Pretorius, South Africa Location : Mabamba Swamp, Uganda Fewer than 5,300 mature shoebill storks are estimated to remain in the wild. Yet Pretorius, while canoeing with a guide, was able to capture these two – likely a breeding pair collecting material for their nest. Despite their name, shoebill storks are actually more closely related to pelicans, herons and ibises. Category : 15-17 Years Photographer : Konrad Gräeter, Germany Location : Baden-Württemberg, Germany Spring sees male blackbirds search for high vantage points to sing and try to attract a mate. This photo was taken in a vineyard at dawn, when the birds sing their most complex compositions. Category: Urban Wildlife Photographer: Seth Forestson, UK Location: Lumphini Park, Bangkok, Thailand Forestson lowered himself onto the mud to capture this common water lizard against the city skyline. These adaptable lizards live in cities across South and South East Asia and will take whatever food is available, such as catfish and koi. Category: Under Water Photographer: Tony Wu, USA/Japan Location: Kagoshima Prefecture, Kyūshū, Japan This is probably the first time the courtship ritual of Abbott's moray eels has been photographed, the NHM said. Wu worked with biologists and used dim red light and a customised fisheye lens to minimise disturbance. Category: Photojournalist Story Award Photographer: Loren Elliott, USA Location: USA San Francisco is estimated to be home to around 100 coyotes, living alongside a large human population. While they can prey on domestic animals, they also help control disease-carrying rodents, and residents' attitudes towards them are mixed. Category: Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles Photographer: Anton Sorokin, US Location: Contra Costa County, California, USA Sorokin dipped his camera and lights in a murky pond to catch this glimpse of a California newt laying her eggs. Category : Behaviour: Invertebrates Photographer: Sitaram Raul, India Location: Thar Desert, Rajasthan, India A scorpion is photographed burrowing into the shifting dunes of India's Thar Desert. Exploring the dunes at night, Raul saw many scorpions searching for prey but as temperatures rose after sunrise, the scorpion dug into the sand to escape the intense heat. Category: Oceans: The Bigger Picture Photographer: Alex Lindbloom, USA Location: Off Cenderawasih Bay, Papua, Indonesia A whale shark investigates the catch of a mobile net-fishing platform, known as a bagan. Lindbloom searched for sharks around dawn, using the bagan's bright lights to illuminate them when there was too little natural light for his drone. Category: Plants and Fungi Photographer: Agorastos Papatsanis, Greece Location: Litochoro, Pieria, Greece Papatsanis used ultrviolet light to illuminate mushrooms known as "beautiful bonnets" growing from a decaying log on the lower slopes of Mount Olympus in Greece. Category: Rising Star Award Photographer: Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas, Germany Location: Germany and Northern Ireland, UK Tinker-Tsavalas uses macro photography to reveal the intricate details of tiny animals that are easily overlooked, particularly in urban habitats. His interest in macro photography developed during the Covid-19 lockdowns, when he was restricted to habitats close to his home in Berlin. Category: Natural Artistry Photographer: Michał Michalski, Poland Location: Litochoro, Pieria, Greece Michalski used a slow shutter speed to photograph birds flying across a background of leafless birch trees. A field of unharvested sunflowers had attracted mixed flocks of birds, especially goldfinches and bramblings, before they were startled into the air by a sparrowhawk. Category: Wetlands: The Bigger Picture Photographer: Alex Visbal, Colombia Location: Stansbury Bay, Great Salt Lake, Utah, USA Visbal documents how a single engineered line can reshape an entire wetland as part of a long-term project on the industrial impact on waterways. The pink comes from microbes thriving in extremely salty water after the area was cut off from fresh water. Category: Photojournalism Photographer: Francisco Negroni, Chile Location: Route 40, Santa Cruz Province, Argentina Negroni records this scene of a dead puma displayed as a hunting trophy in Santa Cruz, a province in Argentine Patagonia. Although Santa Cruz banned puma hunting in 2025, illegal persecution continues. Category: Portfolio Award Photographer: Kutub Uddin, Bangladesh/UK Location: West Sussex, England, UK Uddin's photographs explore the miniature world of slime moulds, organisms that can be barely visible to the naked eye and whose fruiting structures are just one to two millimetres high. A four-year study of children's photographs over the generations and archive material go on display. This is the second year of the UKAHT's three-year mission to protect the historic base on Goudier Island in Antarctica. The winner of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year captures a rarely seen elephant behaviour, revealing the complexity of their emotional lives. title: Lena Dunham's Girls to return for limited HBO run
content: HBO's award-winning show Girls will return to screens for a limited run ten years after the series finale aired. Lena Dunham – the show's creator, writer, and one of its stars – shared the announcement in a mock zoom call with members of the original cast Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet and Andrew Rannells. All five actors, whose careers launched off the back of Girls, will be part of the five-episode revival with production set to begin in 2027. Judd Apatow, who helped get the show green lit with HBO, will also return as executive producer. "We always said we would only return to 'Girls' if there was a specific story we were burning to tell," Dunham said in a statement. "I've missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn't quite picture them in the present day," she said. "Then, right around my 40th birthday, they started talking to me in the shower. And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking it's pretty hard to get them to stop," she said. Girls, which ran for six seasons from 2012 to 2017, was nominated for 19 Emmys and won two, including best casting. It follows the lives of four friends – Hannah, played by Dunham, Marnie, played by Williams, Jessa, played by Kirke and Shoshanna, played by Mamet – living in New York City during their 20s. The show, created by Dunham when she was 23-years-old, attracted both praise and controversy during its airing. The BBC ranked it as number 30 on its 100 Greatest TV Shows of the 21st Century. "We're thrilled to have Lena turn her gaze from the tumult of one's twenties to the milestone of turning forty," Amy Gravitt, executive vice-president of HBO programming, said. "To say the world has changed since we last saw Hannah, Marnie, Shoshanna, Jessa, and Elijah is a massive understatement, but we know fans - old and new - will be happy to see how they've grown and relieved to see that they're still the 'Girls' we knew way back when." The title of the limited run has yet to be announced, but Dunham did ask her fellow cast on the mock zoom call, "can we still call it Girls?", before joking "because we're old as". Other cast and production members, most notably actor Adam Driver, were absent from HBO's official statement. Driver, in his breakout role, played Dunham's on-and-off again love interest in the show. In her 2026 bestselling memoir Famesick, Dunham alleged Driver's on-set behaviour at times turned verbally aggressive and physically imposing. Driver has not publicly commented on the allegations. In Famesick, Dunham also wrote about the breakdown of her working relationship and friendship with co-showrunner and executive producer Jenni Konner. Konner is not included in HBO's statement about the show's revival. Dunham wrote on her Substack that "it's rare in life that you get the chance to return to something you love with new knowledge and a ... ton of gratitude. "I love these girls (and boy) and I love all the people who have reminded us afresh why we do this, which is the joy of being together and the chance to wear yellow mesh…" she wrote. Since Girls ended, Dunham has gone on to create the Netflix series Too Much in 2025 and indie film Sharp Stick. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Turkish police raid opposition TV station, halting live broadcasts
content: Turkish police have raided the headquarters of one of the country's most-watched news channels, halting its live broadcasts. Reports in Turkish media said financial crimes police were searching the building of Halk TV, a pro-opposition channel, and that 11 people had been taken into custody in a raid linked to the channel's owner. The government also appointed a new administrator to run the channel. It is the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his government. Halk journalists were initially unable to get into the building, although they later were allowed in, several reporters said on X. There was a heavy police presence in the building, they said. Halk's news channel and live broadcasts on its YouTube page were both offline early on Wednesday. The channel has been seen by many in the country as being close to the opposition Republican People's Party (CHP). It often voices criticism of Erdoğan's ruling AK party. Prosecutors said arrest warrants had been issued for 17 people as part of the investigation into Halk chairman Cafer Mahiroğlu on allegations of bribery, rigging tenders and money laundering, Turkish media reported. Mahiroğlu, who was reportedly not in the country during the raid, wrote on social media that seven members of his family were among those detained. "Today is a dark day for Turkey," he said in a video message. "The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons." The Istanbul Bar Association denounced the move, which it noted came hours before Ekrem Imamoğlu, widely seen as Erdoğan's biggest political rival, was due to begin his defence against corruption charges in court, for which he has been in prison for over a year. Özgür Özel, leader of the opposition New Party, called the raid "weak and cowardly". "Storming a TV channel with a police raid at dawn and appointing a trustee is something only dictators do," he wrote on social media. Özel set up the party after being removed as the CHP's leader by a court in May and replaced by a party veteran who had previously been voted out, in a move which further cemented Erdoğan's grip on power. Turkey ranked 163rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) 2026 World Press Freedom Index . The organisation stated that 90% of national media outlets were under government control and criticised the "abusive prosecution" of critical publications in the country, which Erdoğan has led since 2003. The vast majority of Turkish media is seen as pro-government after years of state legal and financial pressure, corporate acquisitions and self-censorship. In September, a court ordered the blocking of access to the website and social media accounts of T24, on the grounds that it had published "LGBT propaganda". In October 2025, the authorities seized control of Tele1, another pro-opposition TV channel, appointing a trustee to oversee broadcasts, which were stripped of all hard-news content. The channel still exists but its pro-opposition stance has been completely neutralised. Four years after the attacks, Serhii Kuznetsov appears in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany. Elon Musk's system allows Kyiv to protect Ukrainian skies and effectively guide drones to Russian targets. With few details so far, it is unclear what might need to change for a Pope who has been focused on stability. title: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack
content: The family of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at a wildlife park has paid tribute, describing him as "bright, warm and engaging". William Chapman, 23, visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and was attacked after going into the animal's pen. He was pronounced dead at the scene. In a statement, his family said that he had suffered from "significant mental illness" over a number of years and had been prescribed "strong medication". His family added: "It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death. We would ask everybody to respect that process." City of Doncaster Council has launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death. The park remains closed and a reopening date has not yet been confirmed. "William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved - and William loved them back," a statement released on Tuesday evening said. The family also asked for privacy, saying "the publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time". "The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the statement continued. "The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did." A spokesperson for South Yorkshire Police said Chapman's family were being supported by specialist officers. An inquest is due to open into the death at Doncaster Coroner's Court on Thursday. Footage of the incident has been widely shared on social media, including on Tuesday evening by US President Donald Trump. Downing Street said people should respect the family's views on sharing footage of the incident, but declined to comment on Trump's decision to post the video. The prime minister's official spokesman said: "I think obviously the family have made their position clear. Of course, we respect that position. "I'm not going to comment on the president's social media channels, he's got a press secretary who can speak to that." The incident, which took place shortly after 13:30 BST on Saturday, led to the evacuation and ongoing closure of the park. An eyewitness described seeing Chapman wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in. Mobile phone footage, believed to be from Chapman, appears to show the inside of the enclosure as he approaches the tiger across a patch of grass. Chapman was a former pupil of the Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe. "We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer, during his time with us," the school said in a tribute on Tuesday. "It was a privilege to be part of his journey, and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him." "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with William's family and friends during this incredibly difficult time," the statement continued. As a child, Chapman appeared in the ITV production May Contain Nuts alongside Shirley Henderson - who is best known for playing Moaning Myrtle in the Harry Potter films - and Darren Boyd. He also portrayed Edward Jenner in the BBC series True Stories. Staff at Yorkshire Wildlife Park have separately said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" are with Chapman's family and confirmed the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised. Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to Chapman's family and those who were at the scene. title: Sydney teen charged with murder of boy who was shot in face
content: Australian police have charged a 19-year-old man with murder after a boy, aged 12, was fatally shot in the face and neck at a Sydney home last month. Police were called to a unit in Sydney's northwest on 21 September after reports of a shooting. The boy was rushed to hospital in a critical condition and died three days later. Nine people at the home when the shooting happened were uninjured. Three men - all aged 18 - were arrested and two later released without charge. The third man, Isaac Bechara, who has since turned 19, was initially charged with concealing a serious indictable offence and remanded in custody. On Tuesday, police charged him with murder. Bechara did not apply for bail when he appeared in court on Wednesday. In the immediate aftermath of the shooting, New South Wales (NSW) police ruled out links to organised crime but days later, investigators said they were looking at possible gangland connections. "A number of individuals that were inside the unit at the time are well known to NSW Police and their association with organised crime is being considered by investigators," said Supt Naomi Moore last month. Moore added that some of the people who were present at the time of the shooting were "not currently co-operating with investigators" and that police were yet to recover the firearm. Local media reported that the incident was a suspected accident, citing police sources, and that the boy's father had paid tribute to his son on social media, posting a photo of the pair with the caption, "RIP my baby". When the boy's death was announced, NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said any incident "where we lose a young life in those circumstances is tragic". Goodman Group, the property giant behind the Project Mars data centre, says the decision is due to changes to the "policy and regulatory environment". A man's confession to abducting UK toddler Cheryl Grimmer in Australia was previously thrown out. Wednesday's fatal shooting of a man in his 40s comes after a university student was gunned down on Tuesday. Cheryl Grimmer's family have been petitioning police to consider the new evidence they say they've found. title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
content: Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged. The PM dined with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018 - but this was not detailed in a statement on Monday by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) about his meetings with the club. Burnham has been under pressure to clarify his previous discussions with Man City since the club was found guilty of having "systematically" broken Premier League rules, which it will appeal. The PM, who was mayor until June, sparked widespread controversy when he said last month he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners now sold up. On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade. The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany. It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions". But the statement did not specify that this referred to two hospitality dinners he had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches. A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at £300 for hospitality. Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately £699. Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a £150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018. But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term. BBC News has asked GMCA for more details about this policy - given its website has entries dating back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024. Downing Street has defended the two dinners with Man City's chairman, saying this was hospitality received at home games, which had been declared, rather than separate meetings with the club chairman. But political pressure on Burnham to be clearer about any former discussions with Man City is continuing to mount. Tory shadow sports minister Louie French said: "Andy Burnham promised the country and House of Commons full transparency on his dealings with Manchester City. "This was essential after his inappropriate intervention into football." And Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said "this saga stinks" as he accused Burnham of having apparently "concealed his extensive links to Man City's owners". Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded for several days that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club. Burnham told the Rest Is Politics podcast last week he was "happy" to do this and would "quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester". "None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021." Asked at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday whether anyone at the club had raised the charges they were facing with him or his team, Burnham said: "They did not raise those issues with me." With the PM continuing to face pressure on the issue, he told MPs he was happy for "everything to be set out in full", referring to the GMCA's statement as "a full statement of my key dealings with the owners of Manchester City Football Club". When asked by reporters why the statement did not refer to the two dinners, and what the difference is between "everything" and "key dealings", the PM's press secretary referred back to the GMCA statement. The list of meetings, which was published by the GMCA on Monday, did not include detail on what was discussed. The BBC has asked GMCA why the two dinners were not specifically mentioned. In September Man City - which has dominated the top flight of English football for years - was found guilty by an independent commission of breaching Premier League financial regulations. The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations. Sanctions are yet to be announced and City, which denies any wrongdoing, has lodged an appeal against the verdict. Earlier this month, Sir Richard Leese - who was head of Manchester City Council for 25 years until 2021 - defended a decade-old deal between the council and Man City owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG). Under the partnership between the authority and the company, which is linked to the United Arab Emirates royal family, land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates", according to a University of Sheffield report.
